aAbout: Zoom Earth is an interactive weather map of the world and a real-time hurricane tracker, made by Neave Interactive Limited. It shows near real-time satellite imagery from the NOAA GOES, JMA Himawari and EUMETSAT Meteosat geostationary satellites, updated every 10 minutes, plus HD imagery updated twice a day from NASA's polar-orbiting Aqua and Terra satellites. Around that imagery it layers rain radar with nowcasting, forecast maps for wind, temperature, pressure and more from the DWD ICON and NOAA GFS models, storm tracking using NHC, JTWC, NRL and IBTrACS data, and wildfire heat spots from NASA FIRMS. It runs on the web and as iOS and Android apps, free with an optional Zoom Earth Pro subscription.
aStrengths: Zoom Earth is the better live-weather instrument: satellite imagery every 10 minutes from three geostationary fleets, HD passes twice a day, rain radar with nowcasting, a full set of forecast-model maps, best-in-class hurricane tracking and daily wildfire heat spots — all in one focused, free map that opens with no account. If a storm, a fire or today's clouds are the question, nothing in Google Earth answers it, because Google Earth's planet is always in the past.
bAbout: Google Earth is Google's free virtual globe: high-resolution satellite and aerial imagery, photorealistic 3D cities and terrain, Street View at ground level, and a historical-imagery archive reaching back decades for many places. It adds measurement and drawing tools, KML/KMZ data import and sharing, guided Voyager tours, and Google Earth Studio for cinematic animations. Google Earth Pro — once $399/year — has been free since 2015, and there are no paid tiers. Everything in it is archival: the imagery shows the world as it was when it was photographed, days to years ago depending on the place, not live conditions.
bStrengths: Google Earth is the deeper place explorer by a wide margin: the most detailed photorealistic 3D cities anywhere, Street View at ground level, the deepest historical imagery archive, measurement and drawing tools, KML/KMZ import and sharing, Voyager tours and Earth Studio animations — all permanently free, with no subscription tier at all. For understanding what a place looks like and how it has changed, its scale and familiarity are untouchable.
betterAnswer: They answer different questions. Zoom Earth is better for weather in the present tense: live satellite imagery every 10 minutes, rain radar, forecast maps and hurricane tracking, free with an optional Pro subscription. Google Earth is better for places in the past tense: photoreal 3D cities, Street View and decades of historical imagery, completely free. If you only keep one bookmark, keep the one matching your question — storm-watchers keep Zoom Earth, place-explorers keep Google Earth, and many people keep both.

intro: Zoom Earth and Google Earth both start with a view of the planet from space — and then go in opposite directions. Zoom Earth, by Neave Interactive, is a live weather instrument: satellite imagery updated every 10 minutes, rain radar, forecast maps and a hurricane tracker, free on the web and in mobile apps. Google Earth is the great archive: photorealistic 3D cities, Street View and historical imagery reaching back decades, completely free — but showing the world as it was photographed, not as it is now. One answers 'what is happening?', the other 'what is this place like?'
pricingA: Free on the web and in the apps, with an optional Zoom Earth Pro subscription sold through the app stores. The official US App Store listing checked on 2026-10-29 shows two Zoom Earth Pro price points — $1.99 and $11.99 — but does not label which billing period each price corresponds to, so the billing period for each is unverified and is not stated here. Its Terms of Service say subscriptions are billed on a periodic basis (e.g. monthly or annually), as specified at the time of purchase. No free trial for Pro was stated on the official pages checked.
pricingB: Completely free — Google Earth Pro (once $399/year) has been free since 2015. No paid tiers, no subscriptions; a Google account is optional, needed only for saving places and projects.

verdictA: Choose Zoom Earth if you watch the weather — tracking a hurricane, checking live rain radar, following wildfire smoke, or seeing today's satellite view of your region, on the web or in the mobile apps.
verdictB: Choose Google Earth if you explore places — checking a neighbourhood, a coastline or a building site in 3D, walking streets, measuring land, or watching a familiar place change across decades of imagery.
verdictLine: Zoom Earth is the live instrument — the planet's weather as it happens, refreshed every 10 minutes. Google Earth is the archive — the planet in unmatched 3D detail, as it was. Pick by tense: now, or then.
worldEye: Neither tool shows the ground itself, live. WorldEye takes that third position: a free 3D globe that opens in any browser with no signup — 74,229 public cameras across 109 countries, alongside live flights, ships, satellites, weather, earthquakes and wildfires in the same view. It does not match Zoom Earth's radar and forecast depth or Google Earth's 3D archive, and it does not claim to; it is the live-planet view. Its optional Pro tier is $7.99/week, $13.99/month or $74.99/year.
